source.title: Evaluating Copyright Takedown Methods for Language Models
source.authors: Boyi Wei; Wei-Jia Shi; Yangsibo Huang; Noah A. Smith; Chi-Yuan Zhang; Luke S. Zettlemoyer; Kai Li; Peter Henderson

record.tranche_reason: The study applies several unlearning methods and measures their effects on regurgitation risk and utility, but does not test the recovery attacks in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates unlearning after fine-tuning on NewsQA, but does not try to recover knowledge with post-unlearning fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, or prompt attacks. Its initial fine-tuning creates the memorization scenario; it is not a recovery attack. Table 4 reports aggregate risk-reduction win rates and separate utility metrics for the four unlearning methods.
record.test_reason: In a copyright-takedown setting, the study applies four unlearning methods (GA, GD, KL, PO) to a Llama2-7B-chat model fine-tuned on NewsQA. It measures how far each reduces regurgitation of the forget set and how much general utility (MMLU, MT-Bench) and factual QA survive. This bears on version A's claim that unlearning removes the target while keeping general ability. No recovery attack of any kind is run.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors find that unlearning (notably PO and GD) reduces similarity to blocklisted content. However, all four methods need extensive hyperparameter search and lose about 30–60% of blocklisted and in-domain factual utility. The point that unlearning cannot guarantee content won't be generated again is cited from prior work (Shi et al. 2023; Patil et al. 2023), not tested here. Overall, no takedown method excels on all metrics.
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates four unlearning methods for copyright takedown on Llama2-7B-chat/news memorization; it does not reproduce the recovery-attack protocols named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Unlearning hyperparameters require extensive search; the paper states that outcomes depend on learning rate and training epochs.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning applied to remove verbatim copyrighted text also removes factual (uncopyrightable) knowledge in the blocklisted articles, about 30–60%. The study treats this as a utility loss, not as successful forgetting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning aimed at verbatim regurgitation cannot separate expression from facts; it removes both.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2024 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks
record.problems: Only one model is evaluated in the memorization scenario. Unlearning results use a selected hyperparameter combination after search, and the risk-reduction win rate is an aggregate comparison rather than an absolute accuracy or chance-level measure. No recovery attacks are evaluated.
record.rows_left_out: No applicable results left out; Table 4's unlearning metrics are recorded. Other takedown methods and RAG results do not test the recovery attacks or the unlearning-specific version assessed here.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the unlearned content. Also whether targeted accuracy reaches near chance: the win rates are relative, and the selection rule deliberately kept blocklisted F1 above 40% of the original.
All: no relearning or recovery fine-tuning after unlearning.
All: no activation ablation or deletion-vs-blocking analysis.
All: no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context recovery. The prompts are only hint-completion.
All: RMU and NPO are explicitly not evaluated.

missing.what: Per-metric similarity results for unlearning methods. None of the methods, unlearning included, prevents high semantic similarity to blocklisted text. This is residual leakage after unlearning, relevant to A.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and selection rule. Grid of 25 lr×epoch settings per method; the reported setting was required to keep blocklisted and in-domain utility above 40% of original; about 30 GPU-hours per method.

record.verdict_notes: Single model, single domain for the memorization setting. The vanilla fine-tuned model's MMLU (35.3) is already close to chance, which compresses the utility comparisons. Rows on regurgitation win rate are relative to the other methods (including non-unlearning ones), so they cannot show absolute removal. The study is not an original source for any version.

versions.untested_parts: It does not test recovery attacks, and its risk-reduction win rate does not establish that targeted accuracy reaches near chance. It does measure general utility after unlearning.
No post-unlearning relearning set or recovery fine-tuning is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access-blocking versus deletion is tested.
No quantization of unlearned weights is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
No method is tested for resisting the recovery attacks listed in the claim.

relationships.condition: UnlearningGD and UnlearningKL on fine-tuned Llama2-7B-chat, NewsQA memorization
relationships.reason: Both reduce regurgitation but are not ability-preserving. MMLU falls to 15.8/17.6 (below 25% chance), MT-Bench to 1.5, and in-domain F1 by about 60% (r7, r8, r10, r12, r13, r15).
relationships.display_finding: MMLU fell to 15.8/17.6, below 25% chance, MT-Bench fell to 1.5, and in-domain F1 declined about 60% despite reduced regurgitation.

relationships.condition: UnlearningPO and UnlearningGA on fine-tuned Llama2-7B-chat, NewsQA memorization
relationships.reason: PO keeps MMLU (33.1 vs 35.3) but loses half of MT-Bench and about 40% of in-domain F1. GA reduces regurgitation least (30.3 win rate) and loses ability (r1, r2, r3, r5, r17, r18, r20).
relationships.display_finding: PO kept MMLU at 33.1 versus 35.3 but lost half its MT-Bench score and about 40% of in-domain F1, while GA reduced regurgitation least with a 30.3 win rate and also lost ability.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
